For instance, HVAC systems require regular filter changes, as well as a seasonal maintenance of other components, such as clearing dirt and debris from outdoor components. Similarly, water heaters ac- cumulate build-up from particulate matter in the water which reduces their performance and can lead to their eventual failure. • Wear and Tear: Some components degrade from extended use or old age. Batteries are a good example of such degradation in a wide range of devices. While they are easy to change for some devices (e.g. ther- mostats), they are very difficult and expensive to replace for others (e.g. EVs). • Deprecation: This can affect hardware and software alike. For communications hardware, telephone lines and serial port have shifted to fiberoptic, ethernet, and wireless communications. 3.3 New Features In some cases, the introduction of new features is the main driver of equipment lifecycle decisions. • Retrofit limitations: In some cases, retrofitting updated equipment, or components, is a possibility, e.g. it is relatively easy to change thermostat settings in a building, and it is possible to add blind spot alerts to a vehicle through after market modifications. But other equipment is more challenging to retrofit, such as replacing large, commercial HVAC equipment, upgrading electrical infrastructure, or increasing building insulation. • Compatibility requirements: A new technology may require specific features (e.g. a specific communication protocol) to operate properly in its environment. Older devices may not have compatible features to integrate, or integrate easily, with the new technology. • Standards evolution: While standards aim to establish a unifying set of expectations for specific technologies, they can change over time. This is especially relevant for emerging technologies in sectors with very fast- paced innovation, such as autonomous vehicles. 13 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications 3.4 Budget Budgetary concerns influence decisions about equipment, maintenance, and upgrades at every scale. These finan- cial constraints often shape choices that affect the efficiency, durability, and interoperability of systems over their lifecycle. 3.4.1 Funding Cycles Organizations in the public sector often rely on grants to upgrade their infrastructure. These grants can be limited in available funds and may not be sufficient to upgrade all equipment at the same time. As a result, these organizations can experience deferred maintenance and a slower timeline to upgrade equipment due to the timing of secured grant funding. 3.4.2 Income Lower income households may upgrade their devices at a slower rate than higher income households, and may choose to go with less advanced but more affordable models of devices. 3.5 Public Perception Public perception can be a driver for upgrades in technology. For example, cities may prioritize optimizing traffic corridors with big delays. To support these improvements, equipment upgrades may be necessary.
